source.title: Spectra 1.1: Scaling Laws and Efficient Inference for Ternary Language Models
source.authors: Tejas Vaidhya; Ayush Kaushal; Vineet Jain; Francis Couture Harpin; Prashant Shishodia; Majid Behbahani; Yuriy Nevmyvaka; Irina Rish

record.tranche_reason: The study fits validation-loss scaling laws over parameter and training-token sweeps, using a power-law form similar to the cited scaling-law work, but applies it to ternary models and also compares with 16-bit models.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted validation-loss laws and fit statistics for TriLMs and FloatLMs, plus downstream MMLU comparisons across token counts and model sizes. It does not report a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or tests of predictions from small runs on much larger runs. Inference-speed results are outside the claim.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Hoffmann-style parametric loss law, L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, by least squares on final validation losses. It does this for a ternary quantization-aware LM sweep (99M–1.1B params × 20–150B tokens) and for a 16-bit comparator sweep. This is the original method in a new setting (ternary weights), and the paper compares the fitted exponents across precisions. It also reports downstream MMLU for models trained on 1.2T versus 300B tokens. It does not run a held-out extrapolation test or derive a compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TriLM validation loss falls faster with training tokens than with parameters (β 0.81 vs α 0.32). For FloatLMs the two exponents are nearly equal, and the constant and coefficients differ by precision. Spectra-1.1 models trained to 1.2T tokens show sustained downstream gains and are competitive with FloatLMs at a given compute budget. The remainder of the paper concerns packing schemes and inference kernels.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Hoffmann-style additive validation-loss scaling form and least-squares fits, but applies it to ternary quantization-aware models and compares with 16-bit models; it does not derive a compute-optimal allocation law.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted coefficients and exponents differ between ternary and 16-bit precision settings.
record.problems: The loss fits are evaluated on the same suite of model/data conditions used to fit them, not on held-out larger runs. The scaling-law sweep is limited to 99M–1100M TriLM parameters and 20B–150B tokens; the paper also notes that its pretraining scale was constrained by compute. No compute-optimal split is evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results left out. Inference-kernel speed and packing benchmarks were omitted because they do not measure the scaling-law claim.

untested.parts: Loss as a function of compute is not fitted. The range covers about one decade in N and under one in D, not several orders of magnitude.
Entirely untested. There is no out-of-sample prediction of larger runs; the 1.2T-token models' losses are not compared with the law.
Entirely untested. No compute-optimal N/D split is derived.
Entirely untested. There are no other modalities, no repeated data and no fine-tuning. Ternary QAT is still text pretraining.
No predictive fit of downstream accuracy on scale or loss is evaluated quantitatively. The comparisons are only directional and confounded.
Parameter counting, schedule, data and fitting method are not varied. Curvature away from a single power law is not tested.

missing.what: Fig. 1 plots MMLU vs training FLOPs, with fitted trend lines for Spectra-1 and Spectra-1.1 alongside other model families. This is a downstream-vs-compute fit, but no fit statistics are given.
Table 4 gives per-benchmark downstream scores for the 1B/2B/3B Spectra-1.1 models, with mostly monotone gains across size (e.g. ARC-e, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, SciQ). No row records the size trend.
The claim that the 3B model keeps improving up to 1.2T tokens (intermediate checkpoints) is stated without numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T3. The fitting method matches Hoffmann, but the main result is in a new setting (ternary QAT). The FloatLM fit alone would be T1-like. The authors use the large β to justify data-heavy training, but never check the law's prediction for the 1.2T-token runs. That would have been a V2 test. FloatLM sizes in Appendix C.1 look 10× the TriLM sizes and may be a reporting error.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits loss dependence on parameter count and training tokens, but does not fit loss as a function of compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecking.
No out-of-sample test in which laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts or fitted compute-optimal allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer study.
The study compares MMLU performance across token counts and model sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship from pretraining loss to downstream performance.

The study compares fitted laws across ternary and 16-bit precision, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method, nor test for curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Spectra-1.1 1B
rows.operation_detail: Compare downstream MMLU average accuracy with the Spectra model at comparable size

conditions.value: Spectra-1.1 trained on 1.2T tokens; comparator Spectra trained on 300B tokens

rows.note: The authors state that Spectra-1.1 performs consistently better across the compared parameter sizes; the figure does not provide extractable numerical values here.
rows.check: The value is readable, not figure-only: Table 4 gives Spectra-1.1 1B MMLU (cont.) average 32.34±0.39. The 300B-token Spectra comparator values appear only in Fig. 4. The comparison is confounded: data mix, tokenizer, hyperparameters and exact sizes all differ between Spectra and Spectra-1.1. So it does not isolate token scaling.

relationships.condition: Ternary (TriLM) and 16-bit (FloatLM) pretraining sweeps, ~1 decade in N and <1 decade in D, in-sample fits
relationships.reason: The additive power law in N and D fits final validation loss with R² 0.9921 (TriLM) and 0.9958 (FloatLM) (R1–R4). The range is narrow and the fits are in-sample only.
relationships.display_finding: Additive power-law fits achieved final validation-loss R² of 0.9921 for TriLM and 0.9958 for FloatLM within the sampled narrow ranges.

source_check.condition: Ternary (TriLM) and 16-bit (FloatLM) pretraining sweeps, ~1 decade in N and <1 decade in D, in-sample fits
source_check.reason: R1–R4 establish additive power-law fits with R² = 0.9921 and 0.9958 in the tested ranges. Several-order scaling and larger-run extrapolation remain untested.

relationships.condition: Weight precision varied (ternary vs 16-bit), same fitting procedure
relationships.reason: Exponents differ markedly: α 0.32 vs 0.56 and β 0.81 vs 0.53. For TriLMs the data term dominates, while FloatLM exponents are nearly equal (R1, R3). The difference here comes from model class/precision rather than fitting choices.
relationships.display_finding: TriLMs yielded α=0.32 and β=0.81 versus FloatLM's α=0.56 and β=0.53, making the data term dominant for TriLMs while FloatLM exponents were nearly equal.

source_check.condition: Weight precision varied (ternary vs 16-bit), same fitting procedure
source_check.reason: R1 and R3 report α/β = 0.32/0.81 versus 0.56/0.53, supporting setup-dependent exponents. The paper establishes faster decay of the TriLM token term; it does not establish that this term dominates total loss or isolate precision from the different listed size ranges.

relationships.condition: MMLU at ~1.5B, ~2.5B, ~3.6B ternary models; 1.2T-token Spectra-1.1 vs 300B-token Spectra, and across sizes
relationships.reason: MMLU average rises with size (32.3→34.4→36.1) and is higher at 1.2T tokens at each size (R5–R7). This shows direction only: data, tokenizer and hyperparameters also change, and no predictive fit is evaluated.
relationships.display_finding: MMLU increased from 32.3 to 34.4 to 36.1 with size and was higher at 1.2T than 300B tokens at each size, alongside data, tokenizer, and hyperparameter changes.

relation.reason: Reports original validation-loss scaling fits, differences between fitted exponents, and downstream performance across model sizes and training suites.

tranche.reason: Applies the established additive parameter/data loss form to ternary pretraining, a new precision setting, with its own fitted results and a 16-bit comparator.
